Summary This section introduced the foundations of temporal networks and the problem formulation of TLP. Temporal networks are modelled as temporal graphs, where the evolution of nodes, edges, and attributes can be described in either discrete-time or continuous-time paradigms, each offering different trade-offs between efficiency and information preservation. TLP extends traditional link prediction by requiring models to capture both spatial and temporal dynamics for forecasting future interactions. We further distinguished between transductive and inductive inference tasks, highlighting their respective assumptions and generalisation scopes. Overall, this background sets the stage for understanding the methodological developments reviewed in the following sections. In particular, the distinction between discrete-time and continuous-time representations, as well as between transductive and inductive inference tasks, provides the foundation for the taxonomy that follows. Taxonomy The Framework of the Taxonomy This survey proposes a taxonomy framework for TLP. It contends that all TLP methods comprise two sub-tasks: representing temporal networks and making predictions, which are processed by two distinct components: the Representation Unit and the Inference Unit. The representation unit captures the network structure and dynamics, whilst the inference unit leverages these representations to forecast future links. As depicted in Fig. 5 a, nodes, edges, and attributes are processed by a representation unit to produce inputs that capture dynamic patterns. Subsequently, the inference units process features or embeddings derived from the representation unit to infer future links. In [ 26 ], transductive and inductive tasks relate to inference units but not to graph representation. Fig. 5 The framework of the taxonomy This survey categorises TLP methods based on their underlying elements, despite many approaches being hybrid, combining different representation and inference units or integrating general machine learning strategies. Figure 5 a shows that each method incorporates at least one representation unit and one inference unit. Since temporal networks can be modelled as either discrete-time or continuous-time dynamic graphs, and TLP tasks can be either transductive or inductive, methodologies are classified into four distinct categories based on these combinations, as illustrated in Fig. 5 b.
